assets/audio/this/intro.mp3.text: Look at the picture. This is my house. We say this when something is near us. Notice: this is for one thing. That is for one thing far away. These are for several things near us. Let's practice with a house, a book, and a family. Now ask: Is this your house? You can answer: Yes, this is my house. Or: No, this isn't my house. Great. You can now use this pattern to point to things around you.

assets/audio/have/intro.mp3.text: Imagine someone asking about your work. You say: I have a good job. Here, have means something belongs to you, or is part of your life. You can say: I have a laptop. Or: I have an idea. To ask a question, say: Do you have a job? To make it negative, say: I don't have a car. For he and she, use has. She has a good job. But listen carefully: I have to work means I must work. Have and have to are different patterns.

assets/audio/got/intro.mp3.text: A friend tells you some happy news: I've got a job! In this sentence, I've got means I have. Both can describe possession in the present. Listen: I have a job. I've got a job. In informal conversation, I've got can sound natural. Ask: Have you got a ticket? Answer: Yes, I've got one. For she, say: She's got a ticket. Be careful: I've got to leave now is different. It means I have to leave now.
